title: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
summary: Reuse one block of layers many times to get depth without parameters: halting, why loops compute, Huginn's prelude-core-coda design, random-depth training, a hands-on build, test-time loops and learned depth.
outcomes: Explain why a (k x L) looped model has k layers of parameters but kL layers of compute and depth
Compute ACT halting steps, remainders and mixing weights for a sequence of halting probabilities
Explain how a looped block can run an iterative algorithm and why path independence matters
Describe the prelude, core and coda design and why the input is re-injected at every iteration
Explain how random iteration counts and truncated backprop make training memory independent of depth
Turn a small GPT into a recurrent-depth model and measure accuracy against test-time iterations
Trace Mixture-of-Recursions routing and KV caching, and compute Ouro's exit step from gate outputs
Choose when looping helps (reasoning over context) versus hurts (memorization, latency)

lessons.title: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys

blocks.md:
A GPT is a stack of $L$ distinct transformer blocks. Each token's vector passes through every block once, so the number of blocks is also the number of sequential refinement steps the model can apply before it must predict. Call that number the model's **depth**.

Many reasoning problems are multi-step: add 32 numbers, follow a chain of 16 references, resolve `a=b, b=c, c=?`. A fixed-depth model gets a fixed number of steps. Today there are two standard ways to get more: add layers (more parameters, more memory, more data to fill them) or let the model write out intermediate steps as chain-of-thought tokens (needs reasoning demonstrations to train on and a long context to hold them).

A **looped transformer** offers a third way. Take a small block $f$ of $k$ layers and apply it $L$ times to the same hidden states, feeding each output back in as the next input. The weights are identical on every pass. Saunshi et al. (2025) write this model as $(k \otimes L)$: $k$ unique layers, looped $L$ times.

Unrolled, a $(k \otimes L)$ model is just a $kL$-layer transformer whose groups of $k$ layers are forced to share weights. So it has the **parameters** of a $k$-layer model but the **depth and compute** of a $kL$-layer model.

blocks.tex: f^{(L)} = \underbrace{f \circ f \circ \cdots \circ f}_{L \text{ times}}, \qquad \text{params} \propto k, \qquad \text{FLOPs per token} \propto kL
blocks.caption: A (k x L) looped model: one k-layer block applied L times. Parameter count follows k; compute and sequential depth follow kL.

blocks.title: Twelve distinct blocks versus one block looped twelve times

scenes.caption: A standard 12-layer model: each block has its own weights and is visited once. Depth 12, parameters of 12 blocks.
A (1 x 12) looped model keeps only one block. Its output is fed back as its own input.
Each pass applies the same weights again. The hidden state changes; the parameters do not.
After 12 passes the head reads the final state. Same depth and roughly the same FLOPs as the 12-layer stack, one twelfth of the block parameters.
Side by side: unrolled, the looped model is a 12-layer stack in which every block is a copy of f.

blocks.md: Concrete numbers. A GPT-2-small-shaped layer with width $d = 768$ has about $12d^2$ matrix weights ($4d^2$ in attention, $8d^2$ in the MLP; ignoring biases, norms and embeddings). The count comes from the matrix shapes: attention has four $d \times d$ matrices (the query, key, value and output projections), so $4d^2$, and the MLP widens each vector from $d$ to $4d$ and back with two $d \times 4d$ matrices, so $8d^2$. In total: $12 \times 768^2 = 7{,}077{,}888$, about 7.08M per layer. Twelve distinct layers hold 84.9M. A $(1 \otimes 12)$ model holds 7.08M, yet each token still goes through twelve layer applications, so its matrix-multiply FLOPs per token (about 2 per weight per application: each weight does one multiply and one add per token) are the same as the 12-layer model's.

blocks.prompt: Saunshi et al. trained models to add 32 three-digit numbers with no chain-of-thought. A 12-layer model scores 100%. A 1-layer model scores 0.0%. What does a 1-layer model looped 12 times score?
blocks.reveal:
**99.6%.** The same 1-layer block, applied 12 times, nearly matches the 12-layer model with one twelfth of its parameters. The 2-layer model looped 6 times scores 99.5% while the plain 2-layer model scores 38.8%.

The lesson the authors draw: this task needs **depth** (many sequential steps), not many parameters.

blocks.title: Adding 32 three-digit numbers: accuracy (%)

scenes.caption: Shallow non-looped models fail on 32 operands: 0.0%, 38.8% and 60.7% for 1, 2 and 3 layers (Saunshi et al. 2025, Table 1).
Loop each small model up to an effective depth of 12 and accuracy jumps to 99.6%, 99.5% and 96.6%, close to the 12-layer baseline. Parameter counts are unchanged.

blocks.md: The same pattern holds on Saunshi et al.'s synthetic grade-school math (i-GSM, adapted from Ye et al. 2024). Each problem is a randomly generated graph of quantities written in symbols, where each quantity is computed from others, so answering takes a chain of arithmetic steps. All arithmetic is done modulo 7 (keeping only the remainder after dividing by 7), which keeps numbers small so the difficulty lies in the number of steps; guessing scores about 14%. On it, the 8-layer model scores 73.2%, the 1-layer model 24.5%, and the 1-layer model looped 8 times 73.2%. On these problems, depth is the bottleneck and looping supplies depth cheaply.

Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.
A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

blocks.question: You convert a 12-layer model into a (1 x 12) looped model of the same width. Which statement is correct?
options: Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs stay about the same
Parameters stay the same and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Both stay the same because the unrolled graph is identical
blocks.explain: The looped model stores one block instead of twelve, so parameters drop about 12x. But each token still goes through twelve block applications, so FLOPs (and latency) are about the same. The unrolled graph has the same shape, but its weights are tied, which is exactly what removes the parameters.

blocks.question: On i-GSM, (1 x 8) scores 73.2%, (8 x 1) scores 73.2% and (1 x 1) scores 24.5%. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Looping only helps because it adds parameters
The task is limited by memorized knowledge, so parameters matter most
The task mainly needs sequential depth; parameters beyond one layer add little here
Looped models are always as good as deep models on every task
blocks.explain: The looped model has the parameters of (1 x 1) but matches (8 x 1), so what the extra layers provided was depth, not capacity. That does not generalize to every task: later in the course you will see that knowledge-heavy tasks do need parameters.

lessons.title: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule

blocks.md: The idea is older than modern LLMs. **Universal Transformers** (UT), by Dehghani, Gouws, Vinyals, Uszkoreit and Kaiser (2018; Google Brain, DeepMind and the University of Amsterdam), apply one transformer block recurrently. A recurrent neural network (RNN), which reads a sequence one token at a time and carries a state forward, recurs over **positions** (token 1, then token 2). A UT recurs over **revisions**: at every step it refines the vectors of all positions in parallel, using the same weights each time.

Each UT step has two sub-steps. First, self-attention lets every position read every other position. Second, a **transition function** (a position-wise feed-forward network, or for some tasks a separable convolution, which filters each feature along the sequence on its own and then mixes features, cheaper than a full convolution) is applied to each position. Both the attention weights and the transition weights are tied across steps. Residual connections, dropout and layer normalization wrap each sub-step, as in the original transformer.

blocks.caption: One UT step in words: add the coordinate embedding P^t to the states, run multi-head self-attention, add the residual and layer-normalize; then apply the transition function, add the residual and normalize again. H^t holds one d-dimensional vector per position after step t.

blocks.md: Because the block is shared, it needs a way to know which step it is on. UT adds $P^t$, the sum of a sinusoidal **position** embedding (as in the original transformer: a fixed vector of sines and cosines of the position at many frequencies, so every position gets a distinct pattern with no learned weights) and a sinusoidal **timestep** embedding computed the same way for step $t$. Keep this in mind: the later recurrent-depth LLM deliberately does *not* tell its block the step number.

UT's second idea is **dynamic halting**: let each position decide how many steps it needs. It borrows **Adaptive Computation Time** (ACT) from Graves (2016). At each step $n$, a small sigmoid unit outputs a halting probability $h^n$ for each position. The position keeps running until the running sum reaches $1-\epsilon$ (Graves used $\epsilon = 0.01$); the step where that happens is its halting step $N$. The small $\epsilon$ is there so a position can stop after one step: a single sigmoid output never reaches exactly 1. The leftover mass at the final step is the **remainder** $R$. The output is a weighted mix of the per-step states, with weights $h^1, \dots, h^{N-1}, R$. A position that halts early has its state copied forward unchanged while the others keep going.

To stop the model from always running many steps, training adds a **ponder cost** $N + R$ to the loss, times a small coefficient. $N$ counts the steps but is a whole number with no gradient; $R$ carries the gradient, and since $R$ is 1 minus the earlier halting probabilities, lowering it pushes those probabilities up, so positions learn to halt sooner.

blocks.tex: N = \min\Big\{n : \sum_{i=1}^{n} h^i \ge 1-\epsilon\Big\}, \qquad R = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} h^i, \qquad s = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} h^i s^i + R\, s^N
blocks.caption: ACT halting (Graves 2016) in words: N is the first step where the halting probabilities add up to at least 1 minus epsilon, R is what is left of 1 before that step, and the output mixes the step states with those weights, which sum to 1.

blocks.title: ACT on three positions (epsilon = 0.01, halt at 0.99)

scenes.caption: Step 1. Halting probabilities are 0.995, 0.6 and 0.2. 'the' already crosses 0.99, so it halts after one step with remainder 1 (nothing was accumulated before).
Step 2. 'cat' outputs 0.5: 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1 crosses 0.99, so it halts with remainder 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. 'the' is copied forward. 'sat' reaches 0.5.
Step 3. Only 'sat' is still running: 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8, below the threshold.
Step 4. 'sat' adds 0.4: 1.2 crosses 0.99, so it halts with remainder 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. All positions have halted, so the loop stops.
Final mixing weights per step (each row sums to 1): 'the' uses 1 x step 1; 'cat' uses 0.6 and 0.4; 'sat' uses 0.2, 0.3, 0.3 and remainder 0.2. Ponder costs N + R are 2, 2.4 and 4.2.

blocks.prompt: UT with ACT was run on bAbI, a set of synthetic story-question tasks. Some questions need one supporting fact from the story, others two or three. Would you expect the average number of steps per position to differ between those task types?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The average ponder time was **2.3 +/- 0.8** steps for one-fact tasks, **3.1 +/- 1.1** for two-fact tasks and **3.8 +/- 2.2** for three-fact tasks. The model learned on its own to spend more refinement steps when more reasoning hops are required, and to halt early on irrelevant facts.

blocks.md:
Results that made the paper influential:

- **Translation.** On WMT14 English-German (the English-to-German news translation task of the 2014 Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation), UT base (fixed steps, no ACT) scored 28.9 BLEU (a 0 to 100 score of how many runs of 1 to 4 words in the output also appear in a human reference translation) versus 28.0 for Transformer base with the same parameter count. ACT marginally hurt on translation.
- **Length generalization.** Trained on copy, reverse and addition strings of length 40 and tested on length 400, UT beat both long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, RNNs whose gates control what the state keeps, and transformers by a wide margin, though it was still far from perfect.

- **LAMBADA.** In this dataset the last word of a passage can only be guessed using context from the whole passage, not just the final sentence. UT with dynamic halting set a new state of the art. It averaged 8.2 steps, and fixed-step UTs with 8 or 9 steps did not match it, suggesting halting also acts as a regularizer.

The paper also shows that, under certain assumptions, a UT is Turing-complete (given enough steps and memory, it can simulate any computer program, because its number of steps can grow with the input), unlike a fixed-depth transformer, whose number of steps is capped by its layer count.

blocks.title: Trained on length 40, tested on length 400

scenes.caption: Character accuracy on 400-symbol strings (Dehghani et al. 2018, Table 4). The shared, repeatable block generalizes much further past the training length.
Whole-sequence accuracy is much harsher: one wrong symbol fails the sequence. UT reaches 0.35, 0.46 and 0.02; addition stays mostly unsolved.

blocks.md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

blocks.question: A position's halting unit outputs 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 at steps 1 to 3, with epsilon = 0.01. When does it halt and what is its remainder?
options: Step 2, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.4
It never halts because the sum never equals exactly 0.99
blocks.explain: Running sums are 0.3, 0.8, 1.2. The first to reach 0.99 is step 3, so N = 3. The remainder is 1 minus the sum before the halting step: 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The step-3 halting probability (0.4) is replaced by the remainder so the weights sum to 1.

blocks.question: Which parameters does a Universal Transformer share across its recurrent steps?
options: Only the feed-forward transition; each step has its own attention
Only the attention; each step has its own transition
Both the self-attention and the transition function
Nothing; it shares weights across positions only, like any transformer
blocks.explain: In UT both the self-attention and transition weights are tied across steps, which is what makes the number of steps changeable. (Every transformer already shares weights across positions; that is not what makes UT recurrent.)

lessons.title: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 showed that looping helps on multi-step tasks. This lesson asks why a single block, applied again and again, can represent a multi-step algorithm at all.

Start with a tiny program: `a = 7; b = a; c = b; d = c`. To know `d` you must resolve three references in order. Attention can do one such lookup per layer in the simplest construction: the line `c = b` attends to the line that defines `b` and copies what is known there. So a stack of $L$ layers can resolve about $L$ references, and a block looped $r$ times can resolve about $r$, with the same weights each time.

blocks.title: One reference per loop: a chain of 8 variables

scenes.caption: Before any loop: only a holds a value, because its right-hand side is the literal 7. Every other line points at another variable.
Loop 1: every line looks up the line that defines its right-hand side and copies whatever value is known there. Only b finds one.
Loop 3: the known values have moved three lines down the chain. One loop, one more reference resolved.
Loop 7: h, seven references from the literal, is finally known. Depth needed = chain length minus one.
Loop 8 and later change nothing: every line already holds 7. The state has stopped moving, which is a fixed point; extra loops are harmless.

blocks.md: That is the core intuition: **an iterative algorithm is one step repeated**, and a looped block is one learned step repeated. Giannou et al. (2023) made it precise. They hand-set the weights of a 13-layer transformer and run it in a loop. The input sequence works like a punch card holding instructions, memory and a scratchpad. Each pass executes one instruction of a tiny one-instruction computer (a SUBLEQ-like instruction: subtract, then branch if the result is at most zero), the way a CPU executes one instruction per cycle. Their looped model runs a calculator, a small linear-algebra library and an in-context backpropagation routine, and its depth does not grow with the program's length. This is a statement about what weights *can* do, not about what training finds.

blocks.prompt: Resolving one reference per loop, a chain of 8 variables needs 7 loops. Suppose instead every variable may also replace its pointer with its pointer's pointer each loop. How many loops does the chain of 8 need now?
blocks.reveal:
**3.** After loop 1 each unresolved variable points 2 lines back, after loop 2 it points 4 back, after loop 3 the whole chain is resolved. This trick, **pointer jumping**, doubles the reach per loop, so depth grows like $\log_2$ of the chain length.

Saunshi et al. (2025) prove the transformer version for their p-hop task (follow p references back through a sequence): looping a 1-layer block $\lfloor \log_2 p \rfloor + 2$ times suffices, which matches the depth lower bound known for non-looped models.

blocks.title: Pointer jumping: each loop doubles the reach

scenes.caption: Same program, a different rule: if the variable you point to has a value, copy it; otherwise point to whatever it points to (two links in one step).
Loop 1: b copies 7 from a. Every other variable now points two lines back (c to a, d to b, and so on).
Loop 2: c and d copy 7. The rest now point four lines back (e to a, h to d).
Loop 3: e to h copy 7. Eight variables in 3 loops instead of 7: reach doubles per loop, so depth grows like log2 of the chain length.

blocks.md: Saunshi et al. also connect looping to chain-of-thought. Chain-of-thought is itself a loop: each step runs the whole model and appends **one** new token, which later steps can read. A looped model can instead update the vectors of **all** positions on every pass, so one iteration can hold many "latent thoughts" at once. Their Theorem 5.4 proves the formal link in one direction: for any $L$-layer transformer and $m$ chain-of-thought steps, a looped transformer with $L + O(1)$ layers (a constant number more), a slightly wider embedding and a few extra heads, run for $m$ loops on the input plus $m$ placeholder tokens, produces the same output. Each loop plays the role of one generated thought. Saunshi et al. offer this link as their explanation for why looped models do well on reasoning primitives (lesson 8).

A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

Does training find iterative solutions? Yang et al. (2024) tested in-context linear regression: the prompt is $(x_1, y_1, \dots, x_k, y_k, x_{\text{test}})$ with $y_i = w^\top x_i$ for a hidden $w$, and the model must predict $y_{\text{test}}$. The closed-form answer needs a matrix inverse, which is hard for a transformer to express. Gradient descent needs only matrix multiplies, repeated: exactly the shape a loop provides. A 1-layer GPT-2 block looped (width 256, 8 heads, 0.79M parameters) performed comparably to a 12-layer one (9.48M), under 10% of the parameters.

blocks.tex: w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta\, X^\top (X w_t - y) \qquad\text{versus}\qquad Y_{t+1} = M_\theta(Y_t + P)
blocks.caption: Left: one gradient-descent step on least squares, the same update applied every iteration. Right: Yang et al.'s looped transformer M, with the prompt P added back (injected) at every iteration.

blocks.md: Two details from Yang et al. preview the design of Huginn, the 3.5B-parameter recurrent-depth language model of lesson 4. First, **input injection**: they add the prompt $P$ at every iteration. Without it (loop only $Y_{t+1} = M(Y_t)$, starting from $Y_0 = P$), the error grew quickly (the paper says the model diverged) as soon as it ran more loops than it was trained with. Second, they compute the loss only on the last $T$ of the $b$ training iterations (they chose $b = 20$, $T = 15$) to save memory, a form of truncated backpropagation.

Now the **fixed-point** view. If a loop runs until its state stops changing, the final state $s^*$ satisfies $s^* = f(s^*, e)$: applying the block once more returns the same state. Such an $s^*$ is called a **fixed point**. Deep equilibrium models (DEQs; Bai, Kolter and Koltun, 2019) skip the loop and solve that equation directly with a root-finding method, which they describe as equivalent to running an infinitely deep weight-tied network. They backpropagate through the solution with implicit differentiation (taking the gradient from the equation $s^* = f(s^*, e)$ itself instead of from stored iterations), so training memory stays constant, roughly one layer's activations, however many iterations the solver used.

blocks.title: A contractive loop forgets its start; an integrator does not

scenes.caption: Start at s0 = -4 with e = 1. The contractive update gives -1, 0.5, 1.25, 1.625, ... and approaches 2 = 2e. The integrator just counts up from -4.
Start at 0: 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, ... The contractive loop heads to the same 2. The integrator ends somewhere else because it remembers where it started.
Start at 6: 4, 3, 2.5, 2.25, ... Again 2. Each step halves the distance to the fixed point, so after 8 steps every start is within 0.04 of it.
Change the input to e = 2.5: the fixed point moves to 5. The answer depends on the input, not on the start. That is path independence.

blocks.md:
**Path independence** (Anil et al., 2022) is the property the plot shows: the loop reaches the same steady behavior (a fixed point, or a repeating cycle) from any starting state, given enough iterations. Their own example: $x_{t+1} = x_t + 1$ is path dependent, while $x_{t+1} = (x_t + 1)/2$ always ends at 1. Across tasks, they found that models measured as more path independent did better when given far more test-time iterations than in training; input injection improved path independence, and regularizers that rewarded or punished it raised or lowered accuracy on harder problems.

This explains two choices in Huginn: the state starts from random noise, so the model cannot rely on a particular start, and $e$ is re-injected every iteration, so the end point depends on the input.

Convergence is not automatic. The toy update halves the distance to its fixed point each step (it is **contractive**); a learned block carries no such guarantee. Some loops diverge, and Huginn's analysis (lesson 7) finds tokens whose states orbit or drift instead of settling.

A last consequence: **length generalization**. Fan et al. (2025) trained looped decoders with input injection on tasks whose known algorithm needs more steps for longer inputs: parity of $n$ bits in $n$ steps, copying $n$ symbols in $n$ steps, adding two $n$-digit binary numbers in $n + 1$ steps. Training used lengths up to about 20 and supervised only the final answer after the required number of loops. At test time the loop ran for more steps, chosen either from the known count or by stopping at the most confident step, and the models handled longer inputs than they were trained on, where fixed-depth baselines (including a 20 times deeper model and one with pause tokens) did not.

blocks.question: Which update is path independent, converging to the same state from every start?
blocks.explain: 0.5 s + e halves the distance to its fixed point 2e every step, so every start converges there. s + e keeps adding (the start is never forgotten), 2s + e doubles the distance and diverges, and s = s keeps whatever it started with.

blocks.question: Saunshi et al. show the p-hop task can be solved by looping a 1-layer block floor(log2 p) + 2 times. How many loops does that give for p = 32?
blocks.explain: log2 32 = 5, plus 2 gives 7. The doubling trick is why the count grows with log2 p rather than with p: a one-hop-per-loop solution would need about 32 loops.

blocks.question: Yang et al. train a looped transformer without input injection (Y_(t+1) = M(Y_t), Y_0 = P). What did they observe when running more loops than in training?
options: Error kept falling, because more loops always help
Error was unchanged, because the state had converged
Error grew quickly (diverged) past the trained loop count
The model refused to run more loops
blocks.explain: Without re-injecting the prompt, the influence of the start fades and the state drifts once the loop count leaves the trained range. With injection, the end point stays tied to the input, which is the same reason Huginn feeds e into every iteration.

lessons.title: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda

blocks.md: In 2025, Geiping, McLeish, Jain, Kirchenbauer, Singh, Bartoldson, Kailkhura, Bhatele and Goldstein (ELLIS Institute Tuebingen, University of Maryland, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory) scaled a depth-recurrent decoder to 3.5B parameters and about 800B tokens on the Frontier supercomputer. The released model is **Huginn-0125**. The goal: scale test-time compute by thinking in the continuous hidden space, instead of by generating more chain-of-thought tokens.

The model has three groups of standard causal decoder layers:

- **Prelude** $P$: embeds tokens and runs a few layers to produce $\mathbf{e}$, a latent encoding of the input.
- **Core recurrent block** $R$: the looped part. It takes the current state $\mathbf{s}_{i-1}$ *and* $\mathbf{e}$ and returns $\mathbf{s}_i$.
- **Coda** $C$: a few layers plus the tied output head that turn the final state into next-token probabilities.

The starting state is random noise, and the loop count $r$ can be chosen freely on every forward pass.

blocks.caption: The recurrent-depth forward pass (Geiping et al. 2025, Section 3.1). States have shape n x h: one h-dimensional vector per token.

blocks.title: One forward pass of a recurrent-depth model

nodes.label:
Adapter A
concat(s, e) to h

scenes.caption: The prelude runs once per token and produces e. It never loops.
The state starts as random noise, not as e. Starting from noise pushes the model toward a result that does not depend on where the state began.
Iteration 1: the adapter concatenates s and e (2h features) and maps them back to h, then the 4 core layers update the state.
Each further iteration feeds s_i back with the same e. Same weights every time; only the state changes.
After r iterations, the coda reads s_r and predicts the next token. r = 32 gives 2 + 4 x 32 + 2 = 132 effective layers.

blocks.md:
Why re-inject $\mathbf{e}$ at every step? The authors use gradient descent as the analogy: to minimize a function of variable $\mathbf{x}$ and data $\mathbf{y}$, every step uses $\mathbf{y}$. If the data were only given at the start (say $\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}$), the iteration's end point would depend only on that starting point, and the loop could not act like a stable optimizer over the input.

They also tried two alternatives: adding fresh noise at every step (did not help), and giving the core block the current step number (as UT's timestep embedding does). The step-aware block hurt **path independence** (lesson 3: the end state does not depend on where the state started) and produced models that could not extrapolate to more iterations.

Inside each group, layers are standard: causal self-attention with RoPE (base 50000), a gated SiLU MLP and RMSNorm.

- **Rotary position embedding (RoPE)** encodes position by rotating each pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token's position, so attention scores depend on how far apart two tokens are. Pair $j$ turns by $\text{base}^{-2j/d}$ radians per position ($d$ is the head width), so a larger base gives slower rotations that stay distinct over longer distances.
- A **gated SiLU MLP** computes $\mathrm{SiLU}(xW_g) \odot (xW_u)$ and projects it back with $W_d$, where $\mathrm{SiLU}(z) = z \cdot \mathrm{sigmoid}(z)$ and $\odot$ multiplies element by element. One branch acts as a learned gate on the other, and it uses three weight matrices instead of two.
- **RMSNorm** divides each vector by its root mean square (the square root of the mean of its squared entries) and multiplies by a learned scale per feature. Unlike LayerNorm it does not subtract the mean, which makes it a little cheaper.

To keep the recurrence stable at scale, every layer uses a **sandwich** norm layout: normalize the input of each sublayer *and* the output of each residual sum. The core block also ends with an RMSNorm, so the state handed to the next iteration has a controlled scale.

blocks.caption: The sandwich layer used in every block of Huginn, in words: each sublayer normalizes its input (n_1, n_3) and the residual sum after it is normalized again (n_2, n_4). All four are RMSNorms.

blocks.md:
The production shape is $(l_P, l_R, l_C) = (2, 4, 2)$ with width $h = 5280$ (55 heads of 96), MLP width 17920, a 65,536-token vocabulary and 4096-token sequences. The paper reports about 1.5B parameters in prelude plus coda, 1.5B in the core and 0.5B in the tied embedding. A quick check of the core: each layer has $4h^2 \approx 111.5$M attention weights (query, key, value and output matrices) plus $3 \times h \times 17920 \approx 283.9$M MLP weights (the three matrices of the gated MLP), about 395M, and four layers give about 1.58B.

The model card's rule of thumb: running $r$ iterations behaves like **materializing $1.5r + 2$ billion parameters**: each iteration adds another pass through the 1.5B core, while the 2B of prelude, coda and embedding are used once. At $r = 32$ that is 50B, which is where the paper's "compute equivalent to 50B parameters" claim comes from.

blocks.title: Effective size grows linearly with the loop count

scenes.caption: Huginn's numbers: 1.5B core, 2B everything else. r = 32, the training mean, unrolls to about 50B parameters' worth of compute while only 3.5B are stored.
A smaller core (0.5B) still grows linearly, just with a shallower slope. Compute per token scales with core size x r, while memory for weights stays fixed.

blocks.md: Huginn is scored on standard benchmarks, and the next results use four of them. **GSM8K** is a set of about 8,500 grade-school math word problems, graded on the final number. **ARC** (the AI2 Reasoning Challenge) is grade-school science multiple choice, split into an Easy set and a Challenge set of questions that simple retrieval and word co-occurrence methods got wrong. **HellaSwag** asks for the most plausible ending of a short everyday scene, with wrong endings machine-generated to fool models. **SciQ** is crowd-sourced science exam questions. The multiple-choice sets here have four options, so random guessing scores 25%.

blocks.prompt: Huginn was trained with a random number of iterations averaging about 32. If you run the final model with r = 1, how does it do compared with r = 32?
blocks.reveal:
It collapses. On GSM8K with chain-of-thought prompting, r = 32 scores 34.8 to 42.1% (depending on the answer-matching rule) while r = 1 scores 0.0. ARC-Easy drops from 69.9 to 34.9.

The authors also note that r = 1 barely improved between the 180B-token and 800B-token checkpoints: the later gains live in the iterations of the core block, not in the prelude or coda.

blocks.title: Same data, same setup: recurrent versus fixed depth (Table 4)

scenes.caption: ARC-Challenge. At 180B tokens the recurrent model at r = 32 beats its fixed-depth twin (29.2 vs 27.0). At r = 1 it is near chance (23.7). By 800B tokens r = 32 reaches 38.2.
HellaSwag shows the same shape: 37.3 fixed, 48.8 recurrent at r = 32 after 180B tokens, 65.2 after 800B. With one iteration the model is near chance either way.

SciQ (fact recall): 80.6 vs 73.2 at 180B. Above chance (25) that is a 1.15x gain versus 2.1x on ARC-Challenge (GSM8K, with no chance floor, is 5x raw), so the paper calls the models more similar here.

blocks.md: Getting there was not smooth. The first large run used parameter-free norms, no embedding scale and a plain additive adapter $A(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{e}) = \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}$. It stalled: the hidden states of all tokens became almost perfectly correlated (**representation collapse**), because each iteration mixed the sequence a bit more. The second run (pre-norm, learned adapter) recovered from collapse but learned to **ignore the incoming state**: validation perplexity was the same at 1 and 32 iterations. The third run, with the sandwich layout and a lower learning rate, trained smoothly and kept improving with more iterations.

A looped model can quietly stop using its loop. If it learns to ignore $\mathbf{s}$, extra iterations do nothing. Track validation loss at several iteration counts (Huginn tracked 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64) during training, not just at the default.

blocks.question: A colleague simplifies the design: set s0 = e and stop feeding e into later iterations. What does the paper's reasoning predict?
options: Nothing changes, because e is already inside s0
The loop becomes less stable: its end point depends on the starting point, not on continued use of the input
Training becomes cheaper and generalizes better because the adapter is removed
The model becomes a Universal Transformer and gains Turing completeness
blocks.explain: The authors argue the input must be injected at every step, as data enters every step of gradient descent. With e only in the initial state, the iteration cannot behave like a stable, input-dependent operator; its result depends on the boundary condition.

blocks.question: Using the model card's rule (materialized params = 1.5r + 2 billion), what does running Huginn at r = 16 correspond to, and how many effective layers is that?
options: 26B and 68 layers
24B and 64 layers
26B and 64 layers
50B and 132 layers
blocks.explain: 1.5 x 16 + 2 = 26 billion. Effective depth is 2 prelude + 4 x 16 core + 2 coda = 68 layers. 50B and 132 layers is the r = 32 point.

lessons.title: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop

blocks.md: If you always train with $r = 32$, the model learns to be good at exactly 32 iterations, and running it with 64 at test time is out of distribution. Geiping et al. instead sample a **random iteration count for every training sequence** and minimize the expected loss over both data and iteration counts. This trains one set of weights that works across a range of depths.

blocks.caption: In words: the training loss is the next-token loss averaged over training sequences x and over loop counts r drawn from Lambda. m_theta(x, r) is the model's output with r iterations, and x' is the sequence shifted left (the next tokens).

blocks.md:
The distribution $\Lambda$ is a **log-normal Poisson**: draw a log-rate $\tau$ from a normal, then draw a Poisson count with rate $e^\tau$, then add 1 so $r \ge 1$. A **Poisson** count with rate $\lambda$ is a random whole number (0, 1, 2, ...) whose mean is $\lambda$, like the number of events from a process that fires $\lambda$ times on average. Drawing the rate on a log scale keeps it positive and skews it toward long tails.

Where the mean comes from: if $\tau$ is normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, then $e^\tau$ has mean $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$. Choosing $\mu = \log \bar r - \sigma^2/2$ cancels the extra term, so the rate has mean exactly $\bar r$, the Poisson count has mean $\bar r$, and adding 1 gives $\bar r + 1$. With target mean $\bar r = 32$ and $\sigma = 1/2$, the mean of $r$ is $\bar r + 1 = 33$. Most draws are below 32, with a heavy tail of occasional long runs.

blocks.caption: The minus one half sigma squared term makes the log-normal rate have mean r-bar exactly.

blocks.title: Iteration counts sampled during training (2 million simulated draws)

scenes.caption: Share of training sequences per bucket of r, from our simulation of the paper's sampler (r-bar = 32, sigma = 0.5). The 17-32 range holds about 44% of draws.
The skew: the median is 29 and 55.8% of draws are below 32, yet 5.8% exceed 64 and the 99th percentile is 94. The model regularly sees much deeper unrolls than average.

blocks.md:
A heavy tail creates a memory problem: backpropagating through 94 iterations would store activations for all 94. The fix is **truncated backpropagation**: run all but the last $k$ iterations under `no_grad` (PyTorch's mode that computes without recording the graph backward needs, so their activations are freed at once) and backpropagate only through the last $k$. Huginn fixes $k = 8$. Activation memory and backward compute are now bounded by $k$, independent of how large $r$ is. (A common rule of thumb puts backward at about twice the forward cost, because each layer computes two gradients, one for its input and one for its weights, each a matrix multiply as large as the forward one.)

The prelude still learns every step, because its output $\mathbf{e}$ is injected into each of the last $k$ iterations, so gradient flows back to it through all of them. This mirrors truncated backpropagation through time for RNNs, applied to depth instead of time.

blocks.title: The training-time sampler and loop (simplified from the released code)
blocks.code:
import math, torch

def sample_iterations(mean=32, k=8, sigma=0.5):
    mu = math.log(mean) - sigma**2 / 2
    rate = math.exp(torch.normal(mu, sigma, (1,)).item())
    p = torch.poisson(torch.tensor(rate)).item() + 1
    n_no_grad = max(p - k, 0)   # iterations without gradient
    n_grad = min(k, p)          # last k iterations keep gradients
    return int(n_no_grad), int(n_grad)

def forward(x, model):
    e = model.prelude(x)                  # gets gradients
    s = model.random_state_like(e)
    n_no_grad, n_grad = sample_iterations()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(n_no_grad):
            s = model.core(model.adapter(torch.cat([s, e], -1)))
    for _ in range(n_grad):
        s = model.core(model.adapter(torch.cat([s, e], -1)))
    return model.coda(s)                  # loss on next tokens

scenes.caption: Start of a training step: run the prelude once to get e. This part always receives gradients.
The state starts as random noise shaped like e.
Sample the depth. mu = ln 32 - 0.125 = 3.341. Suppose the normal draw gives a rate of 19.4 and the Poisson draw gives 19.
Split p = 20 into 12 iterations without gradient and the last 8 with gradient.
The first 12 iterations run under no_grad: no activations are stored for backward. They just move the state forward.
The last 8 iterations record the graph. Backward will run through these 8 and, via e, into the prelude.
Had the draw been p = 3, there would be 0 no-grad and 3 grad iterations; for p = 70, 62 and 8. Stored activations never exceed 8 iterations.
The coda reads the final state and the loss compares against the next tokens.

blocks.title: Work per training step at three sampled depths (simplified)

scenes.caption: r = 3: all three iterations keep gradients. Assuming backward costs about 2x forward (a common rule of thumb), backward takes 6 core-pass units.
r = 20: 12 cheap no-grad iterations, then 8 recorded ones. Backward covers only the 8 recorded iterations: 16 units.
r = 70 (a tail draw): forward work grows to 70 passes, but the recorded part and backward stay at 8 iterations. Memory per step is the same as for r = 20.

blocks.md: What truncation leaves out: the no-grad iterations get no direct gradient, so the core is only trained on how it improves states earlier iterations produced. Truncated backprop through time has the same known bias toward short-range effects (Tallec and Ollivier 2017). Random $r$ softens it: the gradient window starts from states refined anywhere from 0 to about 90 iterations, though with $\bar r = 32$ only about 1.4% of draws ($r \le 8$) include the noise start itself.

Two systems details follow from this design.

- **Locked-step sampling.** With thousands of data-parallel workers, each drawing its own $r$, everyone would wait for the worker with the deepest unroll. Huginn samples one $r$ per micro-batch (the slice of data one worker runs through forward and backward at a time) and synchronizes it across workers.
- **More FLOPs per parameter.** Because weights are shared, even the 3.5B model fit with plain data parallelism (every GPU holds a full copy of the weights and processes different data) plus optimizer-state sharding (each GPU stores only a slice of the optimizer's running statistics), with no tensor parallelism (splitting each weight matrix across GPUs). The paper reports 52 to 64 TFLOP/s per GPU (41 to 51% of achievable) on 4096 GPUs (each a chip of an AMD MI250X card, which holds two), with a global batch of 16M tokens per step.

Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

blocks.question: With k = 8, a training step happens to draw r = 100 instead of r = 20. What happens to activation memory for the core block?
options: It grows about 5x, because there are 5x more iterations
It stays about the same, because only the last 8 iterations are recorded
It drops, because the no-grad iterations free memory used by earlier steps
Training crashes, because the sampler is clamped to at most 64
blocks.explain: Only the last k = 8 iterations build the autograd graph, so stored activations are bounded by 8 iterations regardless of r. Forward compute does grow with r (100 passes instead of 20). The sampler has no clamp; tail draws above 64 happen about 5.8% of the time.

blocks.question: Gradients flow only through the last 8 core iterations. Why does the prelude still get trained on every step?
options: It does not; the prelude is frozen after warm-up
Because the coda shares weights with the prelude
Because the no-grad iterations are re-run with gradients at the end of the step
Because e is injected into every iteration, including the last 8, so gradients reach the prelude through each of them
blocks.explain: The adapter concatenates s and e at every iteration. During the last k recorded iterations, the loss depends on e through k paths, so the prelude receives gradient from all of them. Only the tied embedding is shared between input and output head, not the prelude layers.

lessons.title: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth

blocks.md:
Time to build one. The plan: take the `Block` from the GPT you built in the prerequisite course (nanoGPT's pre-norm attention plus MLP), split a tiny model into a prelude (1 block), a looped core (2 blocks) and a coda (1 block), and add the three ingredients of lesson 4 and lesson 5: the concat-then-project adapter, a noise start, and random depth with truncated backprop.

It needs a task where depth matters. We use **variable-assignment chains**, the programs from lesson 3: four chains such as `x3 = 7; x9 = x3; x1 = x9`, interleaved at random but always defined before use. Each line is one position (its embedding is the sum of a left-side and a right-side embedding), and the model must output, at every line, the digit that variable ends up holding. A line's **depth** is how many references it must follow: 0 for `x3 = 7`, 2 for `x1 = x9`.

blocks.caption: The whole architecture change, about 20 lines on top of nanoGPT's Block. The full script (data generator, training, evaluation) ran on an Apple-silicon laptop; every number below is from that run.

blocks.md:
Two details carry over from Huginn. The adapter sees the state and the input side by side and learns how to mix them. The core ends in a normalization so the state handed to the next iteration has a fixed scale.

One detail is new (Huginn uses RoPE): there is no position embedding. Lookups are by name, and causal attention already gives order, which lets the same model read programs longer than any it was trained on.

blocks.code:
def sample_r(mean=8, sigma=0.5):        # log-normal Poisson, as in lesson 5
    tau = random.gauss(math.log(mean) - sigma**2 / 2, sigma)
    return int(torch.poisson(torch.tensor(math.exp(tau)))) + 1

K = 4                                    # backprop through the last 4 iterations
for it in range(3000):
    lhs, rhs, y, _ = make_batch(128)     # 4 chains of 1 to 8 lines each
    r = sample_r()
    out = model(lhs, rhs, max(r - K, 0), min(r, K))
    loss = F.cross_entropy(out.flatten(0, 1), y.flatten(), ignore_index=-100)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step(); sched.step()             # AdamW, lr warms up to 1e-3, then decays (OneCycleLR)
blocks.caption: Training: one depth r per batch from the log-normal Poisson sampler (mean about 9), gradients only through the last 4 iterations. Chains in training have 1 to 8 lines, so depths 0 to 7.

blocks.md: Setup: width 64, 4 heads, 218,698 parameters, batch 128, 3000 steps. For comparison we train a plain 20-layer model (1 + 2 x 9 + 1 layers, the same FLOPs as the looped model at its average depth) with 1,010,058 parameters on the same data. To test, we build 512 programs whose chains have up to 12 lines, so depths 8 to 11 never appeared in training, and score every line at a chosen $r$.

blocks.prompt: The looped model trained with about 9 iterations on average and never saw a chain deeper than 7. At test time, what happens to accuracy on depth 10-11 lines as you raise r from 8 to 16?
blocks.reveal: **It rises from 66.8% to 98.4%.** Deeper chains need more iterations, and the model keeps resolving references for as long as you let it loop. The 20-layer fixed model, which matched it on trained depths (99.6% on depth 6-7), scores 64.0% on depth 10-11 and has no knob to turn.

blocks.title: Accuracy per line by chain depth as test-time r grows

scenes.caption: r = 1: lines that hold a literal or one reference are right; deeper lines sit near 39%, about what you get by guessing the most common of the 4 chains' starting digits (38%).
r = 2: depth 2-3 jumps to 98.9%. Each extra iteration resolves roughly one or two more references (the core has 2 attention layers).
r = 4: depth 4-5 reaches 98.5%. The frontier of solved depth moves right as r grows, as in the one-reference-per-loop picture of lesson 3.
r = 8 (about the training mean): every trained depth is solved, and depth 8-9, never seen in training, is already at 97.7%.
r = 16: unseen depths 8-9 and 10-11 reach 99.2% and 98.4%. Extra test-time iterations buy longer chains than training contained.
r = 32 (and 64, identical): nothing changes. The state has reached its fixed point, so over-running the loop is harmless.

blocks.md: Next, a training-free early exit that lesson 7 discusses for Huginn. Run the loop, read the coda's prediction after every iteration, and stop each line at the first iteration where the KL divergence between successive predictions drops below $5 \times 10^{-4}$. The **KL divergence** $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_x p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ is 0 when two distributions are identical and grows as they differ, so a tiny value means one more iteration barely moved the prediction.

blocks.code:
# run 64 iterations once, keep every state, read each one out through the coda
# model.readout(h) = head(ln_f(coda(h)))
logp = [F.log_softmax(model.readout(h), -1) for h in states]
exit_it = torch.full(y.shape, 64); done = torch.zeros(y.shape, dtype=torch.bool)
for i in range(1, 64):
    kl = (logp[i-1].exp() * (logp[i-1] - logp[i])).sum(-1)   # KL(p_prev || p_now)
    new = ~done & (kl < 5e-4)            # Huginn's threshold
    exit_it[new] = i + 1; done |= new
blocks.caption: Per-line KL exit, from the evaluation script (states holds the core state after each of 64 iterations).

blocks.title: KL early exit: iterations used per line, by depth

scenes.caption: Mean iteration at which the KL rule fired: 2.6, 3.8, 5.8, 8.1, 10.4, 12.7. Deeper lines think longer, with no training for exits at all.
Accuracy at the exit point: 100, 99.9, 99.8, 99.5, 98.1, 94.2%. Exits are a little early for the deepest unseen chains, probably because a prediction can stall for a step before its last change.

blocks.md: Path independence (lesson 3) can be checked directly: run the same programs from two different noise starts and measure the distance between the two final states. In our run the mean distance per line was 0.931 after 4 iterations, 0.365 after 8, 0.009 after 16 and 0.002 after 32. The starts are forgotten, which is why r = 32 and r = 64 give identical answers.

Lesson 4 said Huginn's runs failed in two ways, so the script logs two monitors every 250 steps: validation loss at $r = 1$ and $r = 32$ (if they stay equal, the model ignores its state), and the mean cosine similarity (the dot product of two vectors divided by their lengths: 1 when they point the same way, 0 when unrelated) between different lines' final states (if it climbs toward 1, representations are collapsing). We then retrained with two of the changes Huginn rejected: replacing the adapter with $\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}$, and adding a UT-style sinusoidal step-number signal to the core's input.

blocks.title: The monitor: validation loss at r = 1 versus r = 32

scenes.caption: Step 250 of 3000: both models are still at the start, and extra iterations barely help either (0.88 vs 1.09, 0.92 vs 0.96).
Step 1500: the concat model's r = 32 loss has dropped to 0.033 while r = 1 stays at 0.61. The model that is also told its step number shows 0.564 versus 0.552: it is not using its loop.
Step 3000: 0.534 versus 0.012 for concat, 0.549 versus 0.501 for the step-aware model. The gap between the two numbers is the signal to watch, not either number alone.

blocks.title: Unseen depth 10-11: three variants and a fixed-depth baseline

scenes.caption: At r = 8. The 20-layer model has no r; it scores 64.0% here and 74.2% on depth 8-9 (99.6% on trained depths 6-7).
At r = 16: concat 98.4%, s + e 99.6%, step signal 38.2%. The fixed-depth baseline cannot run deeper, so it stays at 64.0% with 4.6x the parameters.

blocks.md: What the ablations showed, honestly. The step-number variant never learned to use its loop in 3000 steps: its loss was nearly the same at $r = 1$ and $r = 32$ throughout, and deep lines stayed near 40% at every $r$. The $\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}$ adapter, by contrast, trained as well as concat here (99.6% on depth 10-11 at $r = 16$), and no run collapsed: at step 3000 the mean cosine similarity between lines' states was 0.48 for $\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}$ and 0.23 for concat, and every run's highest value (0.51 to 0.60) came at the first check, step 250, then fell. Huginn's collapse appeared in a 3.5B model that also had parameter-free norms and no embedding scale, so a toy cannot reproduce every large-scale failure.

Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

Turning a GPT into a recurrent-depth model takes a split into prelude, core and coda, a concat adapter, a noise start and a random-depth training loop. The monitor that matters is the gap between low-r and high-r validation loss.

blocks.question: During training your recurrent-depth model logs validation loss 0.81 at r = 1 and 0.80 at r = 32, and the gap has not grown for thousands of steps; mean cosine similarity between states is a steady 0.3. What is the most likely problem?
options: The learning rate is too low, so both losses fall slowly
Representation collapse: all token states have become identical
The model has learned to ignore its recurrent state, so extra iterations do nothing
Nothing; equal losses mean the loop has converged
blocks.explain: Equal loss at 1 and 32 iterations means the core's output does not depend on how many times it ran: the model solved what it could without the loop. That was Huginn's second failed run and our step-signal variant. Collapse shows up in the cosine-similarity monitor instead; converged loops still differ sharply between r = 1 and r = 32.

blocks.question: Why could the looped model answer depth-10 lines when the 20-layer model, trained on the same data with about the same FLOPs, could not?
options: It can run more iterations at test time than in training, and each iteration resolves more references
It has more parameters than the 20-layer model
It uses position embeddings that extrapolate
The 20-layer model was trained for fewer steps
blocks.explain: Both models handle trained depths. Only the looped one can be given more depth at test time (r = 16 instead of about 9), and because it learned a repeatable step rather than a fixed pipeline, the extra iterations keep resolving references. It has 4.6x fewer parameters, and neither model uses position embeddings.

lessons.title: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches

blocks.md:
At inference you choose $r$ with an argument (`num_steps` in the released Hugging Face code). More iterations mean more compute per token and, up to a point, better answers. The model card's guidance: fewer than 4 steps gives very coarse answers, benchmarks keep improving up to around 64 steps when there is enough context to reason about, and beyond that more steps generally neither help nor hurt.

The next results are **zero-shot**: the prompt holds only the question, with no solved examples (**few-shot** prompts put a few solved examples first). They include **MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding), four-option questions across 57 subjects from high school to professional level, and **OpenBookQA**, four-option elementary science questions (lesson 8 describes it).

blocks.title: Accuracy as test-time iterations grow (Huginn, zero-shot)

scenes.caption: r = 4: the model is weak across the board (Geiping et al. 2025, Table 1).
r = 8: big jumps everywhere. HellaSwag goes from 43.5 to 58.5.
r = 16: still improving, notably MMLU (25.3 to 31.3).
r = 32: most of these zero-shot tasks have nearly saturated. Harder tasks with more context (math, few-shot ARC) keep using extra iterations longer.

blocks.md: How many iterations a task can use depends on the task and on the context. HellaSwag reaches near peak at about 8 iterations, while GSM8K and HumanEval (164 Python programming problems, graded by running unit tests on the generated code) keep improving further. On ARC-Challenge with no few-shot examples, accuracy saturates around 8 to 12 iterations; with 1 example around 20; with 25 to 50 examples around 32. More context gives the model more to reason about, so it uses more depth.

Fixed $r$ wastes compute on easy tokens. A recurrent-depth model gives you **per-token early exit** without any special training: iterate until the prediction stops changing. Huginn's criterion: compute the next-token distribution after each iteration and stop when the KL divergence between two successive steps falls below $5 \times 10^{-4}$, then sample and move to the next token.

This is the rule you ran on the toy in lesson 6. Read the KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler) as the average extra log-loss, in nats (natural-log units), paid for predicting with $q$ when outcomes follow $p$. Standard transformers need models trained specifically for early exits or extra exit heads for this.

blocks.tex: \text{stop at the first } i \text{ with } \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{i-1} \,\|\, p_i\big) < 5 \times 10^{-4}
blocks.caption: Stop at the first iteration whose next-token distribution differs from the previous one by a KL divergence under 5e-4. The released code also offers rules based on entropy (how spread out the distribution is), the latent state, or the top token staying stable.

blocks.title: Toy early exit: the prediction settles, the KL drops, the loop stops

scenes.caption: Simplified toy (not Huginn): 4 logits updated by s_i = 0.5 s_(i-1) + e, which converges to 2e. After step 1 the distribution is 0.394 / 0.375 / 0.138 / 0.093.
Step 2: A pulls ahead (0.490). KL to step 1 is 2.24e-2, far above 5e-4, so keep going.
Step 3: KL = 5.21e-3. Still above the threshold.
Step 4: KL = 1.25e-3. Close, but still above.
Step 5: KL = 3.05e-4 < 5e-4, so exit. Running to step 12 would barely change anything (0.584 / 0.263 / 0.118 / 0.036): 7 iterations saved.

blocks.md: Evidence that this works zero-shot: on the first 50 questions from several MMLU categories, the number of iterations before exit varied by subject; the model exited earliest on high school mathematics and took on average 3.5 more steps on moral scenarios. On MT-Bench (80 two-turn chat questions whose answers GPT-4 grades from 1 to 10), early exits scored 5.56 versus 5.66 with a fixed 32 iterations, a difference well inside the standard error of about 0.39.

Early exit creates a **KV-cache** puzzle. Every iteration of every core layer writes its own keys and values for each token, so the cache has one entry per token per iteration. If an earlier token exited at iteration 7, a later token at iteration 20 finds no entry at depth 20. Huginn's answer: attend to the **latest, deepest available** entry. The paper's rationale is that all iterations use the same K and V projection matrices on successive states, so the entries "match". That is a design rationale checked empirically, not a guarantee: states at different depths are different vectors. A plausible reason it works here: each core pass ends in a normalization and many states settle toward a fixed point, so late iterations give similar keys.

The same idea enables **KV-cache sharing**: give each token a fixed budget of $k$ cache slots for the recurrence, and at iteration $i$ read and write slot $i \bmod k$. With a budget of 16, iteration 17 overwrites iteration 1's slot. (The released code counts this budget in core-layer cache entries: `compress-s16` keeps 16 entries per token, which is the last 4 iterations of the 4-layer core.)

blocks.title: KV-cache sharing for one token and one core layer (budget k = 4)

scenes.caption: Iterations 1 to 4 write slots 1, 2, 3, 0 (i mod 4). The cache is full.
Iteration 5 maps to slot 1 and overwrites iteration 1's keys and values.
After iteration 8 the cache holds the 4 most recent iterations: 8, 5, 6, 7.

After iteration 10: slots hold 8, 9, 10, 7. Reading the budget as 4 iterations of the 4-layer core, with r = 32 the cache per token drops from 4 + 4 x 32 = 132 layer entries to 4 + 4 x 4 = 20, a 6.6x saving.

blocks.md: The evidence is measured, and model specific. On MT-Bench, Huginn with fixed 32 iterations scored 5.66; with cache budgets of 16, 8 and 4 it scored 5.69, 5.63 and 5.86, all well inside the standard error of about 0.39 (Geiping et al. 2025, Table 6). Ouro, a different looped LM with 4 steps (lesson 9), shows that the choice of which depth to keep matters: in decoding, keeping only the last step's cache scored 78.85 on GSM8K versus 78.92 with every step's cache, but keeping only the first step's cache collapsed to 18.73. During prefill (processing the prompt), every step needed its own cache; reusing one cost over 10 points on GSM8K.

What is the loop actually doing? Geiping et al. track each token's state $\mathbf{s}_i$ over many iterations, plot its distance to the state after 128 iterations, and project trajectories onto their top principal (PCA) directions, the directions along which the states vary most. Convergence speed depends on the token and its context: key words of a question are "deliberated" much longer. They find three recurring shapes. Many tokens **converge** to a fixed point. Some fall into **orbits**, circling in several directions at once. Some act as **sliders**, drifting steadily along one direction. The same shapes appear from different random starts.

blocks.title: Three shapes of latent trajectory (schematic)

scenes.caption: Converge: the state settles to a fixed point, so successive predictions stop changing and the KL exit fires. Huginn reports this for many tokens. Schematic shapes, not measured data.
Orbit: the state circles without settling, seen for harder tokens such as the '3' in a GSM8K question about a 3-egg omelette. A KL exit may fire late or never.
Slider: the state drifts steadily in one direction, seen for a key word like 'wrong'. The authors suggest a drift could let the model count iterations.
Restarting from different noise gives the same shape per token (path independence), so the shapes come from the token and its context, not from the start.

blocks.md:
Two more tricks fall out of the architecture.

**Continuous chain-of-thought.** Instead of starting each new token's recurrence from noise, warm-start it from the previous token's final state $\mathbf{s}_r$, so latent work carries forward between tokens. With the KL exit, mean steps to exit fell from 12.7 to 11.9 on high school mathematics, 14.6 to 13.5 on philosophy, 15.6 to 14.4 on logical fallacies and 16.2 to 16.0 on moral scenarios (Figure 10), drops of 0.2 to 1.2 steps.

**Self-speculative decoding.** Speculative decoding normally needs a separate small draft model. Here the same model drafts the next few tokens with few iterations, then a deeper pass verifies all drafts at once. Draft states are not wasted: verification can continue from them. The paper describes this scheme without measured speedups, so the next figure is arithmetic, not a benchmark.

blocks.title: Draft at r = 4, verify at r = 32 (illustrative arithmetic)

scenes.caption: Plain decoding: each token waits for the previous one, so 4 tokens cost 4 x 32 = 128 sequential core iterations.
Draft: the same model runs only 4 iterations per token, producing 4 guesses in 16 sequential iterations.

Verify: all 4 positions run together, warm-started from their draft states, for 28 more iterations each. If all 4 drafts match the deep predictions, 4 tokens took 44 sequential iterations instead of 128.
If draft 3 disagrees, keep drafts 1 and 2 plus the verifier's own token 3: 3 tokens for 44 iterations versus 96. Verifying 4 positions costs more FLOPs, just not more sequential time.

blocks.md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

blocks.question: Successive-step KL values for one token are 2.24e-2, 5.21e-3, 1.25e-3, 3.05e-4, 7.52e-5 (measured after steps 2 to 6). With Huginn's threshold of 5e-4, after which step does the token exit?
options: Step 4
Step 6
Step 5
It never exits; KL must reach exactly 0
blocks.explain: The first value below 5e-4 is 3.05e-4, measured between steps 4 and 5, so the token exits after step 5. 1.25e-3 (step 4) is still above the threshold.

blocks.question: Using the paper's description (a budget counted in iterations, k = 16), Huginn keeps 16 cache slots per token. Which slot does iteration 33 write, and whose entry does it replace?
options: Slot 1, replacing iteration 17
Slot 0, replacing iteration 32
Slot 1, replacing iteration 1 only
Slot 33, because each iteration gets a new slot
blocks.explain: 33 mod 16 = 1. Slot 1 was written by iteration 1, overwritten by iteration 17, and is now overwritten by iteration 33. That a token can read entries written at other depths is what Huginn's MT-Bench runs support empirically; it is not guaranteed for every looped model.

lessons.title: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space

blocks.md: Looping gives depth without parameters. What does it lose? Saunshi, Dikkala, Li, Kumar and Reddi (Google Research, 2025) pretrained 1B-scale language models on 250B tokens of the Pile (EleutherAI's open 825 GiB English text corpus built from 22 sources such as web pages, books, code and papers) and compared, for each budget $k$: the 24-layer baseline $(24 \otimes 1)$, a $k$-layer model $(k \otimes 1)$ with the same parameters as the looped one, and the looped model $(k \otimes 24/k)$ with the depth and FLOPs of the baseline. They grouped downstream tasks into closed-book QA (answer from facts stored in the weights, so memorization), open-book QA (the needed facts are in the context), math word problems and reasoning primitives.

To compare groups, they define **% Gap**: how much of the distance between the small model and the full baseline the looped model closes. 0% means looping did nothing (parameters are what matter); 100% means looping fully replaces the missing parameters; above 100% means the looped model beats the full baseline.

blocks.caption: Avg_G is the average score of a task group G (Saunshi et al. 2025, Eq. 1).

blocks.title: 6 layers, 6 layers looped 4x, and 24 layers (Saunshi et al. Table 3)

scenes.caption: Closed-book QA (memorization): 11.2 / 4.0 / 8.2. Looping recovers only 58% of the gap; parameters matter for stored facts.
Open-book QA (answer is in the context): 33.9 / 19.3 / 28.7, closing 64% of the gap.
Math word problems: 29.3 / 17.7 / 29.8. The looped model matches the 24-layer one with a quarter of the parameters: (29.8 - 17.7) / (29.3 - 17.7) = 104%.
Reasoning primitives (variable-assignment chains): 47.5 / 24.1 / 56.1. The looped model clearly beats the full baseline, a gap above 130%.
Validation perplexity (lower is better): 7.40 / 9.25 / 8.42. Looping closes only about 44% of the perplexity gap, so perplexity alone undersells looped models on reasoning.

blocks.md: Huginn shows the same split. OpenBookQA is about 6,000 four-option science questions, each built around one fact from a small book of science facts that is normally not shown. In that usual closed-book format Huginn scores 38.2 (the paper's Table 5 setting; lesson 7's chart, from Table 1, shows 38.8), below the 46.2 of OLMo-2 7B, a fully open model from the Allen Institute for AI. When the relevant fact is provided in the prompt, it jumps to 49.2 (+11.0), close to OLMo-2's 53.4. The authors' reading: the recurrent model has less capacity to memorize facts but more capacity to reason about its context. A related 2025 effort, Ouro (Zhu et al.), reports the same theme from controlled experiments: its looped models' advantage comes from better knowledge manipulation, not more knowledge capacity.

Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

The other costs are the ones from lesson 1, now with Huginn's numbers. Each token passes through $4 + 4r$ layers: 20 at $r = 4$, 132 at $r = 32$, 260 at $r = 64$. These passes are sequential, so latency grows linearly with $r$. Without sharing, the KV cache also grows with $r$. And training is touchier: the representation-collapse and ignored-state failures from lesson 4 were real at scale (lesson 6 reproduces both checks on a toy).

blocks.title: The design space of looped transformers

scenes.caption: Axis 1, what to share. UT loops the whole block stack; ALBERT shares parameters across all its layers to shrink BERT, Google's encoder language model (ALBERT stands for A Lite BERT).
Axis 2, where to loop. Middle looping keeps unique first and last layers and loops the middle (Saunshi et al.; the Middle-Cycle variant of Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR); Huginn's prelude and coda).

Axis 3, scratch or converted. Relaxed Recursive Transformers initialize a shared block from a pretrained model (e.g. Gemma 2B to a recursive 1B) and add a small low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a trainable update of two thin matrices, per loop to relax the tying.
Axis 4, how many loops per token. ACT halting (UT), a KL exit rule (Huginn), a learned router (MoR), or an entropy-regularized learned exit (Ouro).

blocks.md: The fourth axis is where the field moved in 2025. **Mixture-of-Recursions** (Bae et al. 2025) learns a router that gives each token its own number of recursions and changes what the KV cache stores; **Ouro** (Zhu et al. 2025) pretrains looped models on 7.7T tokens with a learned exit gate and reports that its 1.4B and 2.6B models match results of up to 12B models on many benchmarks. Lesson 9 works through both, plus the small recursive puzzle solvers HRM and TRM.

blocks.question: You must ship a small on-device model mainly for trivia-style factual QA with no retrieval. Memory is tight, latency matters. Is a looped model a good fit?
options: Yes: looping recovers the full accuracy of a 4x larger model on any task
Not really: closed-book QA depends on stored knowledge, which looping recovers poorly, and every loop adds latency
Yes: looping lowers latency because the weights stay in cache
No: looped models cannot be quantized
blocks.explain: Closed-book QA is the task group where looping closed the least of the gap (58% for k = 6) because it depends on capacity. Loops also add sequential compute. Looping shines on reasoning over context; adding retrieval (moving facts into the context) is the setting where a looped model does better.

blocks.question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
blocks.explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.

lessons.title: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM

blocks.md: Huginn runs every token for the same $r$ unless a training-free KL rule (lesson 7) stops it early. But "the" rarely needs 32 iterations, and the key number in a word problem may need more. Three 2025 lines of work **learn** how much depth to spend: Mixture-of-Recursions learns a router, Ouro learns an exit gate, and the small recursive reasoners HRM and TRM learn to refine an answer over many outer steps.

**Mixture-of-Recursions** (MoR; Bae et al. 2025) shares one stack of layers across $N_r$ recursions, keeping unique first and last layers (their Middle-Cycle scheme, like a prelude and coda). Before each recursion a small router scores every token. In **expert-choice** routing each recursion step acts like an "expert" that picks its own top-$k$ tokens; with hierarchical filtering, only tokens chosen at step $r$ can be chosen at step $r + 1$. To match a balanced budget the capacities shrink as $N_r/N_r, \dots, 1/N_r$: with 3 recursions, all tokens, then 2/3, then 1/3.

blocks.tex: g_t^r = \sigma(\theta_r^\top \mathcal{H}_t^r), \qquad \mathcal{H}_t^{r+1} = \begin{cases} g_t^r\, f(\mathcal{H}_t^r, \Phi') + \mathcal{H}_t^r & \text{if } g_t^r \text{ is in the top-}k \\ \mathcal{H}_t^r & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Expert-choice MoR (Bae et al. 2025, Eq. 2.1, with the percentile threshold written as top-k): a linear router with a sigmoid scores token t at recursion r; selected tokens get the shared block f, scaled by their score, plus a residual; the rest pass through unchanged.

blocks.title: Expert-choice routing: 6 tokens, 3 recursions

scenes.caption: Capacities follow 3/3, 2/3, 1/3 of the tokens: recursion 1 takes all 6, recursion 2 keeps the top 4, recursion 3 the top 2. Everyone runs recursion 1.
The recursion-2 router scores each token from its current hidden state: 0.2, 0.9, 0.6, 0.1, 0.3, 0.8. Top 4: cat, mat, sat, a. 'the' and 'on' stop after one recursion.
Hierarchical filtering: only the 4 survivors are scored again. Scores 0.7 (cat), 0.4 (sat), 0.2 (a), 0.9 (mat); the top 2 are mat and cat.
Final depths 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3: 12 token-recursions instead of 18 for a fixed 3-recursion model. Selected tokens are updated as g f(h) + h, so the router score also scales the update.

blocks.md:
Depth per token creates the KV problem from lesson 7: a token that stopped at recursion 1 has no keys or values at recursion 3. MoR offers two answers.

- **Recursion-wise caching**: at each recursion, store KV only for the tokens active there, and let attention at that depth see only those entries.
- **Recursive KV sharing**: every token passes recursion 1, so cache only there and reuse those entries at every deeper recursion. This saves the most memory, but attention still reads the full-length cache at every depth, so the reads from memory do not shrink.

blocks.title: KV entries in the recursion block

scenes.caption: The example above: a fixed 3-recursion model stores 6 x 3 = 18 entries per shared layer. Caching only active tokens stores 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. Sharing the first recursion's cache stores 6.
As fractions for N_r = 4 recursions (capacities 4/4 to 1/4): (N_r + 1) / 2N_r = 0.625 and 1 / N_r = 0.25 of the fixed-depth cache (Bae et al. 2025, Table 2).

blocks.md:
Expert-choice has a catch for autoregressive models: top-$k$ over a sequence compares a token's score with scores of **later** tokens, which do not exist yet when decoding. MoR adds an auxiliary binary cross-entropy loss that pushes selected tokens' scores toward 1 and the rest toward 0, so each token's own score predicts the selection at inference. The alternative, **token-choice** routing, picks a depth once per token from the first state (no look-ahead) but must be pushed toward balanced loads with a balancing loss.

Results (135M to 1.7B parameters): at equal training compute, an expert-choice MoR with 2 recursions and 167M non-embedding parameters reached 43.1% average few-shot accuracy versus 42.3% for a 315M vanilla model. With 3 recursions, token-choice scored 40.0% against 42.6% for expert-choice, and KV sharing 41.9%.

blocks.question: Expert-choice MoR with N_r = 4 recursions and 8 tokens uses capacities 8, 6, 4, 2. How many KV entries per shared layer do recursion-wise caching and recursive sharing store, compared with 32 for fixed depth?
options: 20 and 8
32 and 8
20 and 2
16 and 4
blocks.explain: Recursion-wise caching stores only active tokens: 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 20, which is (4 + 1) / 8 = 0.625 of 32. Recursive sharing stores recursion 1 only: 8 entries, 1/4 of 32. Sharing saves more memory but every depth still reads all 8.

blocks.md: **Ouro** (Zhu et al. 2025) loops a whole stack of $N$ layers up to $T_{\max} = 4$ times (24 layers for the 1.4B model, 48 for the 2.6B) and attaches an LM head and an **exit gate** to every step. The gate outputs $\lambda_t$, the probability of stopping at step $t$ given it got there. The probability of surviving the first $t$ steps is $S_t = \prod_{j \le t}(1 - \lambda_j)$, so the probability of exiting first at step $t$ is $\lambda_t S_{t-1}$, and the last step takes what is left. At inference the token exits at the first step whose cumulative exit probability reaches a threshold $q$ (a knob set at deployment).

blocks.title: Ouro's exit distribution for one token (T_max = 4)

scenes.caption: The gate outputs instantaneous exit probabilities 0.1, 0.5 and 0.6 at steps 1 to 3 (step 4 needs none).
Exit-first probabilities: 0.1; 0.5 x 0.9 = 0.45; 0.6 x 0.45 = 0.27; and the leftover survival 0.45 x 0.4 = 0.18 goes to step 4. They sum to 1.
Cumulative: 0.10, 0.55, 0.82, 1.00. With q = 0.5 the token exits after step 2, with q = 0.8 after step 3, with q = 0.9 it runs all 4.

blocks.md:
Training the gate is the hard part. Ouro's loss is the expected next-token loss under the exit distribution, $\sum_t p_\phi(t)\, \ell^{(t)}$, minus $\beta$ times the entropy of that distribution. Without the entropy term the gate collapses: deeper steps get more weight, so they train more, get lower loss and pull in even more weight, until every token uses $T_{\max}$. The entropy term (equivalent to a KL toward a uniform prior over steps) keeps the distribution spread so difficulty can decide.

In a second stage the LM is frozen and only the gate is trained, with a label that says continue when one more step still lowered that token's loss by more than about 0.005. On MMLU at an average of 2.5 steps, the stage-two gate scored about 66% versus about 64% for the stage-one gate; for scale, the 1.4B model's full 4-step MMLU score in the paper's Table 7 is 67.35%.

blocks.caption: Ouro stage I (Zhu et al. 2025, Eq. 4): expected loss over exit steps, minus beta times the entropy H of the exit distribution, summed over positions i.

blocks.md: Compare the three exit rules in this course. ACT (lesson 2) adds a ponder cost that always pushes toward fewer steps. Huginn trains with random depth and exits by a KL rule that needs no training. Ouro learns a gate with no built-in preference for shallow or deep, then tunes it on measured loss improvement. Its exit distribution is the one PonderNet (Banino et al. 2021) introduced, which used a KL toward a geometric prior that favors early halting; Ouro swaps in a uniform prior.

blocks.question: An Ouro gate outputs lambda = 0.3, 0.5, 0.2 at steps 1 to 3 (T_max = 4). With threshold q = 0.7, after which step does the token exit?
options: Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
blocks.explain: Exit-first probabilities: 0.3, then 0.5 x 0.7 = 0.35, then 0.2 x 0.35 = 0.07. Cumulative: 0.30, 0.65, 0.72. The first to reach 0.7 is step 3. Note the cumulative value, not the gate's own output, is compared with q.

blocks.md:
**HRM and TRM** are a different kind of model. They are small networks trained from scratch on about 1000 examples of one puzzle type (Sudoku-Extreme, 30 x 30 mazes, and ARC-AGI, the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of colored-grid puzzles, unrelated to the ARC science quiz of lesson 4) with heavy data augmentation, not language models.

The **Hierarchical Reasoning Model** (HRM; Wang et al. 2025, 27M parameters) has two 4-layer transformer modules: a low-level one updated every step and a high-level one updated after every $n$ low-level steps. With $n = 2$ low-level steps per high-level step, repeated for $T = 2$ cycles, one forward pass makes 6 module calls (4 low-level, 2 high-level) and backpropagates only through the last 2, a shortcut the authors justify by assuming the states have reached a fixed point.

The **Tiny Recursive Model** (TRM; Jolicoeur-Martineau 2025) keeps the loop and drops the rest: one 2-layer network that updates a latent $z$ from $(x, y, z)$ six times, then the answer $y$ from $(y, z)$. Both recursive models rely on **deep supervision**: up to 16 outer steps per example, each with its own loss and update, each starting from the previous step's detached state. TRM reports 44.6% on ARC-AGI-1 and 7.8% on ARC-AGI-2 with 7M parameters, against 40.3% and 5.0% for HRM, and, with an attention-free 5M variant, 87.4% versus 55.0% on Sudoku-Extreme.

blocks.title: Tiny Recursive Model training loop (simplified from the paper)

scenes.caption: One network does both jobs. With x in its input it updates the latent z (reasoning); without x it updates the answer y from z.
Two full recursions run without a graph: 14 network calls that only move y and z forward, like Huginn's no-grad iterations.
The last recursion is backpropagated in full (7 calls). With 2 layers per call, that is 3 x 7 x 2 = 42 layers of effective depth per supervision step.
y and z leave detached: the next supervision step starts from them but sends no gradient back into this one.
Deep supervision: up to 16 outer steps on the same example, each with its own loss and optimizer update, each starting from the previous answer.
A halting head q learns whether the current answer is already right; during training a confident q ends this example early so more examples fit in the budget.

blocks.md: Deep supervision is truncated backprop applied across outer refinement steps. Each step's graph is cut where the carried state enters, as Huginn cuts its graph at the no-grad iterations, yet the state keeps improving across steps. How much you backprop through matters: in TRM's ablation, HRM's 1-step gradient (backprop through only the final call of each update) scored 56.5% on Sudoku-Extreme versus 87.4% with the full last recursion.

Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

blocks.question: TRM's effective depth per supervision step is T x (n + 1) x layers. With T = 3, n = 6 and a 2-layer network, what is it, and how much over 16 supervision steps?
options: 42 per step, 672 in total
36 per step, 576 in total
42 per step, 42 in total because the state is detached
18 per step, 288 in total
blocks.explain: 3 x 7 x 2 = 42 layers per supervision step, as in the paper's Table 1, and 42 x 16 = 672 across all steps. Detaching cuts the gradient between steps, not the computation: the answer still benefits from all 672 layers of refinement.
